questions.q: Which laboratory pattern indicates primary hypothyroidism?
ch: Low TSH with a low free T4
Raised TSH with a normal free T4
Low TSH with a raised free T4
Normal TSH with a raised free T4
Raised TSH with a low free T4
questions.exp: Primary hypothyroidism shows a raised TSH with a low free T4: the gland fails and the pituitary drives it harder.
why: A low TSH with low free T4 indicates central hypothyroidism, where the pituitary fails to respond.
A raised TSH with a normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism.
A low TSH with a raised free T4 indicates hyperthyroidism.
A normal TSH with a raised free T4 does not fit primary hypothyroidism.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions?
questions.exp: Hashimoto's chronic autoimmune thyroiditis is the most common cause where iodine is sufficient. Iodine deficiency remains the leading cause worldwide.
why: Iodine deficiency leads worldwide but not in iodine-sufficient areas.
A pituitary lesion causes central hypothyroidism, which is far less common.
Amiodarone is a recognised but uncommon cause.
Congenital agenesis presents in infancy and is rare.

questions.q: Which antibody confirms an autoimmune aetiology for hypothyroidism?
questions.exp: Anti-TPO antibodies confirm Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis.
why: Anti-smooth muscle antibody indicates autoimmune hepatitis.
TSH-receptor antibodies are the marker of Graves' disease, which causes hyperthyroidism.
Anti-nuclear antibody is a non-specific marker of connective tissue disease.
Anti-mitochondrial antibody indicates primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.q: How should levothyroxine be taken to ensure adequate absorption?
ch: On an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
At bedtime with an evening snack
With an antacid to protect the stomach
questions.exp: Levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, separated from calcium and iron. Food, calcium, iron and proton pump inhibitors all impair absorption.
why: Calcium binds levothyroxine and must be separated from the dose.
An evening snack reintroduces the food-absorption problem.
Acid suppression reduces levothyroxine absorption.
Taking it with food substantially reduces absorption.

questions.q: How long after a levothyroxine dose change should the TSH be rechecked?
questions.exp: Recheck the TSH about 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change. Steady state takes weeks and earlier testing misleads.
why: Timing relative to a single dose is not the issue; steady state is.
Three to five days is far short of steady state and gives a misleading result.
A day after a change reflects nothing about steady state.
Six months delays appropriate titration unnecessarily.

questions.q: Why should levothyroxine be started at a low dose in an elderly patient with cardiac disease?
ch: Because the elderly need less hormone overall
Because renal clearance of levothyroxine is reduced
Because the TSH assay is unreliable in older patients
Because absorption is unpredictable with age
Because raising metabolic demand can precipitate angina or arrhythmia
questions.exp: Start low and go slow in the elderly or those with cardiac disease. Restoring metabolic rate raises cardiac demand and can precipitate angina or arrhythmia.
why: The eventual replacement requirement is based on weight and residual function, not simply age.
Levothyroxine is not primarily cleared renally.
The TSH assay remains valid in older patients.
Absorption is affected by food and drugs rather than age itself.

questions.q: A patient presents with hypothermia, bradycardia, hyponatremia and altered mentation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hypothermia with bradycardia, hyponatremia and altered mentation is myxedema coma, an ICU emergency at the severe extreme of hypothyroidism.
why: Septic shock typically causes fever and tachycardia.
HHS is defined by marked hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality.
Thyroid storm is the hyperthyroid emergency, with fever and tachyarrhythmia.
Adrenal crisis causes hypotension and hyperkalaemia rather than this pattern.

questions.q: In suspected myxedema coma with possible adrenal insufficiency, which should be given first?
questions.exp: Give hydrocortisone before levothyroxine if adrenal insufficiency is possible, because thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate a crisis.
why: Giving thyroid hormone first can precipitate adrenal crisis by speeding cortisol clearance.
Glucose alone does not address either hormone deficiency.
Antibiotics treat a precipitant but not the endocrine emergency.
Rewarming alone does not correct the underlying hormone deficits.

questions.q: Which laboratory abnormalities may accompany untreated hypothyroidism?
ch: Hyperlipidemia, hyponatremia, anemia and a raised creatine kinase
Hypolipidemia, hypernatremia and a low creatine kinase
Hypercalcaemia with a suppressed parathyroid hormone
questions.exp: Hyperlipidemia, hyponatremia, anemia and a raised creatine kinase can all accompany hypothyroidism.
why: These are the opposite of the recognised associations.
Polycythaemia is not a feature; anemia is.
Calcium and parathyroid abnormalities are not characteristic.
This acid-base pattern is not associated with hypothyroidism.

questions.q: A patient is investigated for unexplained hyperlipidemia and fatigue. Which single test is most appropriate?
questions.exp: TSH is the most sensitive screening test for primary thyroid disease, and new hypothyroidism can present as hyperlipidemia, hyponatremia or unexplained fatigue.
why: Ultrasound assesses structure, not function.
Uptake scanning is used to investigate hyperthyroidism.
Free T3 is not the screening test for hypothyroidism.
Anti-TPO confirms aetiology once hypothyroidism is established; it is not the screen.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism?
questions.exp: Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition driven by TSH-receptor antibodies, is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
why: A TSH-secreting adenoma is rare.
A toxic nodule causes hyperthyroidism but is less common than Graves'.
Thyroiditis causes a transient thyrotoxic phase and is less common.
Exogenous hormone excess is a recognised but less frequent cause.

questions.q: Which laboratory pattern indicates primary hyperthyroidism?
ch: Suppressed TSH with a raised free T4 or T3
Suppressed TSH with a low free T4
Normal TSH with a low free T3
Raised TSH with a low free T4
Raised TSH with a raised free T4
questions.exp: Primary hyperthyroidism shows a suppressed TSH with a raised free T4 or T3. TSH is the most sensitive marker.
why: A suppressed TSH with low T4 suggests central hypothyroidism or recovery.
This pattern does not indicate hyperthyroidism.
Raised TSH with low T4 is primary hypothyroidism.
A raised TSH with raised T4 suggests a TSH-secreting lesion or assay interference.

questions.q: Which findings point specifically to Graves' disease rather than a toxic nodular goiter?
ch: A tender, painful thyroid with raised inflammatory markers
A solitary palpable nodule with local tenderness
questions.exp: Graves' has the eye disease and pretibial myxedema; a toxic nodular goiter does not. TSH-receptor antibodies or radioactive iodine uptake confirm it.
why: A painful thyroid with raised inflammatory markers suggests subacute thyroiditis.
Low uptake indicates thyroiditis or exogenous hormone, not Graves'.
Contrast exposure may precipitate thyrotoxicosis but is not a Graves' feature.
A solitary tender nodule suggests nodular disease or haemorrhage rather than Graves'.

questions.q: How does radioactive iodine uptake help distinguish causes of thyrotoxicosis?
ch: High uptake indicates thyroiditis and low uptake indicates Graves'
High uptake indicates Graves' or a toxic nodule; low uptake indicates thyroiditis or exogenous hormone
Uptake is always high in thyrotoxicosis regardless of cause
Uptake correlates with the free T4 level rather than the cause
Uptake distinguishes benign from malignant nodules only
questions.exp: High uptake indicates Graves' disease or a toxic nodule, where the gland is actively making hormone. Low uptake indicates thyroiditis or exogenous hormone, where it is not.
why: This reverses the correct interpretation.
Uptake is low in thyroiditis and exogenous thyrotoxicosis.
Uptake reflects the mechanism rather than the hormone level.
Uptake scanning here distinguishes mechanism, not malignancy.

questions.q: Why must a thionamide be given before iodine in thyroid storm?
ch: Because iodine given first supplies substrate and fuels new hormone synthesis
Because iodine causes an allergic reaction if given second
Because the thionamide works only in an iodine-free environment
Because iodine must be given with food
questions.exp: Thionamide before iodine, always. Iodine given first provides substrate for new hormone synthesis and can worsen the storm. Iodine follows at least an hour after the thionamide.
why: Iodine does not inactivate the thionamide.
The sequence is about synthesis, not allergy.
Thionamides work by blocking synthesis and do not require an iodine-free state.
Food timing is not the reason for the sequence.

questions.q: Which antipyretic should be used for fever in thyroid storm, and why?
ch: Aspirin, because it also reduces inflammation
Acetaminophen, because aspirin displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins
Ibuprofen, because it lowers metabolic rate
Aspirin, because it lowers the free T4 level
questions.exp: Use acetaminophen rather than aspirin. Aspirin displaces thyroid hormone from its binding proteins and raises free hormone levels.
why: Fever in storm should be treated, with the right agent.
Aspirin is specifically avoided because it raises free hormone levels.
Ibuprofen does not lower metabolic rate and is not the recommended choice.
Aspirin raises rather than lowers the free T4.

questions.q: A patient on methimazole develops fever and a sore throat. What is the correct action?
ch: Double the dose to control the thyrotoxicosis
Stop the drug and check a full blood count for agranulocytosis
questions.exp: Sore throat and fever on methimazole or propylthiouracil means stopping the drug and checking a full blood count for agranulocytosis.
why: Increasing the dose worsens the risk.
Aspirin is avoided in thyrotoxicosis and does not address the marrow.
Definitive therapy is a later decision; the immediate issue is possible agranulocytosis.
Continuing risks overwhelming sepsis if the count is suppressed.

questions.q: Which thionamide is preferred in thyroid storm and in the first trimester of pregnancy?
questions.exp: Propylthiouracil is preferred in storm and in the first trimester; methimazole is first-line otherwise.
why: Lithium is not a standard thionamide alternative.
Perchlorate is a rarely used second-line agent.
Methimazole is first-line in most other situations but not in storm or the first trimester.
Carbimazole is a methimazole prodrug and carries the same first-trimester concern.

questions.q: How is thyroid storm diagnosed?
ch: By a free T4 rising above a defined diagnostic threshold
By radioactive iodine uptake scanning of the gland
By demonstrating TSH-receptor antibodies in the serum
By the characteristic appearance on thyroid ultrasound
Clinically, for example using the Burch-Wartofsky score, without waiting for labs
questions.exp: Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis, for example by the Burch-Wartofsky score. Do not wait for laboratory confirmation to treat.
why: Hormone levels in storm overlap with uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis and do not define it.
Uptake scanning identifies the underlying cause, not the decompensated state.
TRAb indicates Graves' aetiology rather than storm.
Ultrasound assesses structure, not decompensation.

questions.q: Why are glucocorticoids given in thyroid storm?
ch: To slow the ventricular rate directly during the storm
To improve radioiodine uptake by the thyroid gland
To reduce peripheral T4 to T3 conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency
To block the release of preformed hormone from the gland
questions.exp: Glucocorticoids reduce peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and also cover relative adrenal insufficiency in storm.
why: Steroids do not prevent thionamide-induced agranulocytosis.
Rate control is achieved with a beta-blocker.
Steroids are not given to enhance iodine uptake.
Iodine blocks hormone release; steroids do not.
